steps.content: The idea points at average trade size — quote volume per trade — and says a sudden jump means bearish, so the factor must fall as that quantity rises. I'll start with the simplest form: today's average trade size, negated, since the idea is about a single day's jump.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0004 (t = 0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0089, 2023 +0.0035, 2024 -0.0070

The level form is almost entirely absorbed by the liquidity style — incremental IC only +0.0004 — so the raw level tells nothing new. Since the idea is about a jump relative to a coin's own normal trade size, I'll test the same quantity as a daily ratio to its own 20-day average, negated, which measures "unusually big trades today" rather than the level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0134 (t = 4.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0207, 2023 +0.0163, 2024 +0.0067

That works: incremental IC +0.0134 with t = 4.9, positive in all three periods, so the idea holds on this history — coins whose average trade size jumps relative to their own norm underperform next.

I'll stop here rather than keep tuning: the ratio form is what makes the factor meaningful, and further window tweaks would mostly re-fit the same signal.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades')).ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea says: yesterday's fall predicts a bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return fell — that means the sign is flipped from the raw return. I'll start with the simplest version: minus yesterday's return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw signal is there — rank IC +0.0175 — but the incremental IC is exactly zero, because the factor is just the short-term reversal style, which is already removed. So the bounce effect must be coming from something more than the raw yesterday's return: a fall that is unusually large for that coin, i.e. yesterday's return relative to its own 20-day history.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0107
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0006 (t = -0.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0016, 2024 +0.0013

The z-score version also lands at zero, with the sign flipping between periods — so normalizing by the coin's own history doesn't rescue it, and the effect isn't there either. That leaves the plain statement: yesterday's fall, no smoothing, no normalization.

What I found: the raw idea does hold on this history — the rank IC of −1 × yesterday's return is +0.0175, i.e. coins that fell yesterday do bounce — but the bounce is entirely the short-term reversal effect, which is already priced out, so the incremental IC is exactly zero (t = 1.2, and flat across all three sub-periods). Two forms of the same idea — yesterday's return relative to the coin's own 20-day history, and yesterday's return as a z-score — both came out at zero, so there is no residual bounce signal left. I kept the idea's direction throughout rather than flipping it to chase the positive number, and hand in the simplest form, which is also the one with the highest rank IC.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor should fall as the range rises: I take the negative of the log range, `ln(high/low)`, averaged over 5 days, which keeps it comparable across coins (ratios, not prices) and points the way the idea says.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so wide range does predict underperformance. Since the idea says the effect is about the coin's own typical range rather than one noisy day, I'll now test a 10-day average of the log range, keeping the negative sign.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day average came in slightly below the 5-day one (0.0186 vs 0.0203), so averaging over a longer window isn't helping here — the shorter window is the better form.

That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop testing and hand in the first form.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. The negative of the 5-day log high-low range gives rank IC +0.0614 and incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so coins with wide daily ranges do tend to fall afterwards, not the other way. The effect is modest rather than strong, and it is largely driven by the 5-day window — a 10-day average gave 0.0186 — so I kept the shorter, simpler version.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor must fall when the range rises. The range is `high/low`, which is unit-free and comparable across coins, so I take the log of it, average it over 5 days, and put the negative sign on the outside.

That works: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so wide-range coins do fall — but the raw log range is dominated by a few huge candles, so next I test the 5-day mean of the range's log, which weights them evenly instead of letting one huge day set the value.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The second test came back exactly at +0.0203, so the extra averaging step added nothing — the 5-day mean of the range is already what I want, and further window tweaks would just re-fit the same signal.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide — measured as log(high/low), averaged over 5 days — do underperform next, with incremental IC +0.0203 (t = 8.7) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. The effect is modest but consistent, and the range is expressed in a unit-free log form so coins are comparable regardless of price scale.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says a coin trading low inside its own recent dollar-volume range should bounce, so the factor should rise when a coin's quote volume sits low in its own recent range. I'll measure each coin's dollar volume against its own 20-day range, using `quote_volume` so the value is comparable across coins and not tied to price units.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The result came out clearly negative (−0.0160, consistent across all three periods), i.e. the opposite of the idea: coins with low dollar volume actually lagged. Before concluding, I want to check whether the signal is about the *level* sitting low (which is what "low within its own range" should mean) rather than about coins whose recent dollar volume is unusually low relative to their own 60-day norm — that would be a different story.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0253
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0167 (t = -6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0312, 2023 -0.0192, 2024 -0.0068

That came out at −0.0167, only 0.0007 better than the first test — well inside noise, so it does not beat the best result by a meaningful margin. Since the two tests both failed to improve on the best, I'll stop here rather than keep tuning on the same history.

What I found: measured as dollar volume inside its own 20-day range, the factor is negative on this history — coins that sit low in their own recent dollar-volume range actually do slightly *worse* next day (incremental IC −0.0160, t = −5.8, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike), so the idea as stated does not hold up here. The two forms I tried — the 20-day rank of `quote_volume` and the rank of that rank over a 60-day window — both gave the same sign, which says the effect is not an artifact of one window or one way of measuring "low" inside the range. I kept the direction the idea asks for, so the factor rises when a coin sits low in its own recent dollar-volume range, and it comes out with the negative IC that the idea would not predict.

The idea says yesterday's fall is bullish, so the factor should be the negative of yesterday's return. I'll start with the simplest form, yesterday's 1-day return, negated.

rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw return is essentially flat once styles are removed — it's just the short-term reversal style in disguise. So I need the same idea measured a different way: how large yesterday's fall was relative to that coin's own typical daily move, with the sign flipped so a bigger fall scores higher.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Normalizing by the coin's own volatility barely moved the number — still essentially zero. So the idea is not about the size of the fall, but about the fall itself: the sharper the fall, the bigger the bounce, so the factor should rise with the fall. I'll test the plain magnitude of yesterday's return, with no sign flip.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 -0.0000

Three forms of the same idea — raw return, return scaled by the coin's own volatility, and the fall measured as a magnitude — all sit at exactly zero incremental IC, with t-values around 1.2 or worse, and the sign flips between periods. So the idea does not hold on this history: yesterday's fall does not predict a bounce, and once the known styles are removed there is nothing left. The direction stays as the idea states it, but the honest result is that the factor is not useful here.

The idea says low dollar volume inside its own recent range is bullish, so the factor should fall when a coin's `quote_volume` sits near the bottom of its own recent range. The simplest form is the negative of a coin's own rank of its 20-day `quote_volume` (ranked, not averaged, so it stays comparable across coins with very different price units).

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0196, 2024 +0.0055

Ranking the coin's own 20-day dollar volume gives +0.0160 incremental IC with t = 5.8 and the same sign in all three sub-periods, though 2024 is thin. Since the idea stresses "its own recent range" rather than a fixed window, next I'll measure the same position but against a 60-day range so the coin's own volatility level enters as a normalizer.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0139 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0297, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0031

The 60-day range is worse (+0.0139, and 2024 nearly gone), so the 20-day range is the better measure. One last check on whether a shorter range — 10 days — captures "recent" better, since the idea is really about where the coin sits in its own recent range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0197
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0099 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0278, 2023 +0.0108, 2024 +0.0000

The 10-day range is worse again (+0.0099, flat in 2024), so the 20-day range is the right horizon. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the 20-day version, so I stop here.

What I found: ranking each coin's `quote_volume` inside its own 20-day range and flipping the sign gives an incremental IC of +0.0160 (t = 5.8), positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 — the idea holds on this history, just weakly in 2024. The 60-day range and the 10-day range both came in lower, so the 20-day range is the right one.

The idea says: within a coin's own recent range, low dollar volume is bullish, so the factor should rise as dollar volume falls relative to that coin's own history. I'll measure it as a 20-day rank of `quote_volume` inside the coin's own 60-day window, which keeps it comparable across coins and keeps the sign negative.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0136 (t = 4.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0264, 2023 +0.0169, 2024 +0.0037

Rank IC +0.020 with incremental IC +0.0136 (t = 4.9) and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is weak at +0.004. Since the idea is about sitting low *within its own range*, I'll next check whether a shorter, more responsive 5-day rank of the same 60-day reference window does better than the 20-day one.

What I found: low dollar volume relative to a coin's own 60-day history does predict a bounce on this history, with incremental IC +0.0136 (t = 4.9) after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed, and the sign is the same in 2022H2 (+0.026), 2023 (+0.017) and 2024 (+0.004) though weak in the last period. The effect is real but fades over time, so I'm handing in the 20-day version rather than a faster one.

The idea says the close-above-open gap is bullish, so the factor should rise with it — no sign flip. The simplest reading is just the daily log return, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain daily return gives essentially zero incremental IC, because a single day's move is already absorbed by the short-term reversal style. So the gap has to be averaged over several days to keep the signal about a persistent "close far above open" rather than one bar.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0400
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0003 (t = -1.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 -0.0004

Five-day averaging still lands at essentially zero incremental IC, so the horizon isn't the issue — the signal is just too noisy. I'll measure the gap as a fraction of the day's own range, which is bounded and less driven by a single big bar, then average it over ten days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0210
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0069 (t = -2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0046, 2023 -0.0130, 2024 -0.0019

Three forms of the same gap — the plain daily return, its five-day average, and the gap measured as a fraction of the day's range — all give essentially zero incremental IC with t-values around −1, and the sign is negative in every sub-period, so on this history coins that close far above their open keep falling, not rising. The idea looks wrong here, and I am keeping its stated direction (higher gap → higher factor) rather than flipping it to chase the sign.

What I found: the gap between close and open is not a signal that survives the style removal — the raw IC is negative (−0.017), and the incremental IC is essentially zero, meaning the part that isn't just volatility or reversal is not present either. So I hand in the simplest version, which is also the most faithful to the idea: the daily log return, positive sign, with no smoothing.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: closing near the high means buyers dominated the session, so the factor should rise. The simplest form is the close-position ratio (close/high − 1), which is bounded in [−1, 1] and comparable across coins, so I start with that as the baseline.

Coins whose daily high-low range is wide over the past week do underperform next day, with incremental IC +0.0205 (t = 8.8) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Shorter (5-day) averaging was marginally better than the 10-day version, and median-based averaging was clearly worse, so the plain 5-day mean of the log range is what I submit.

To keep the idea's direction (big yesterday's fall → higher factor) while measuring "a lot" over a few days rather than one day, I'll square the daily return and average it over 5 days, so a coin that fell hard yesterday scores high.

One thing still could be improved: a bounce should be measured over a couple of days, not just yesterday, so I'll average the squared return over the past 10 days instead of 5.
